Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Rachel Owens (Summit Head of ML), Tim Nguyen (Platform Eng), Laura Chen (Security)

Summary (auto):
Quick discovery to understand Summit's migration goals from OpenAI to a Dedicated or Private deployment. Main drivers: cost predictability, latency at scale, data controls. Action: Redwood to send pricing and run eval parity benchmarks vs OpenAI, share security docs.

Topics:
- Current stack and pain points
- Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
- Compatibility with vLLM/TGI and open model variants
- Eval parity and regression concerns
- Security/compliance requirements
- Next steps and POC scoping

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for making time, uh I'm Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Jordan our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Jordan: hey hi all, thanks, excited to dig in.
[00:10] Rachel: thanks Alex, yeah we appreciate it. quick background, we use OpenAI for most gen tasks today, embeddings for search and a few fine-tune-ish prompts, cost has been creeping up and latency at tail is a problem for some interactive features.
[00:27] Tim: yeah TL;DR we need predictable per-token cost, also we run heavy batch jobs for embeddings and nightly fine-tuning prep so throughput matters.
[00:36] Alex: got it, so two buckets: interactive low-latency and high-throughput offline. are you looking at Dedicated to replace hosted OpenAI entirely or hybrid?
[00:46] Rachel: leaning hybrid to start, but want to understand parity — like will outputs match what we see from OpenAI, and how hard is migration for prompt compatibility.
[00:56] Jordan: great q. in our experience model parity depends on model choice and tokenization nuances; for Redwood Dedicated you can run the same open models we host, or bring variants. there can be small scaffolding differences, for example temp/stop sequence handling and tokenization differences if you switch vendor models.
[01:12] Laura: on the security side, main asks: SOC2 Type II, ISO27001, audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and importantly KMS integration for customer-managed keys. also data residency in us-east for now.
[01:25] Alex: absolutely, we can share our security package. Redwood Dedicated supports KMS/HSM integrations, VPC peering and private control plane for our Private offering, and audit logs are available at token/request level in the console.
[01:38] Tim: curious about runtime compatibility — our infra folks built around vLLM for lower latency and TGI for some pipelines. can Redwood Dedicated run those runtimes or do we need to rework?
[01:50] Jordan: good point; Redwood's serving runtime is our own GPU-optimized engine but it's compatible with many transformer families. we do common runtime integrations — we can run models that folks run on vLLM/TGI, but migration usually means re-benchmarking. if you rely on specific vLLM operator behaviors, there might be slight perf differences.
[02:09] Rachel: and eval parity — if we run our internal eval harness, what should we expect? do you provide a reproducible baseline vs OpenAI?
[02:18] Jordan: yes, we can run eval parity tests. typical approach: we run their prompt set at comparable temperature/decoding settings, capture token-level logs, and compare metrics (F1, BLEU, hallucination rates, latency p50/p95). sometimes we need to tweak quantization or kernel selection for latency-cost tradeoffs.
[02:37] Tim: about batching and KV cache — interactive features need small batch low-latency, can we tune batching config per-route?
[02:46] Alex: yep, per-route policies are supported in Dedicated, you can set preferred latency SLOs and we adjust batching and caching heuristics. there are also autoscale/burst options for spiky traffic.
[02:57] Laura: any notes on data retention and log redaction? we can't have raw PII logged in external dashboards.
[03:04] Jordan: we support configurable retention and redaction rules, plus optional on-prem/private control plane so logs don't leave your VPC. for Dedicated we also offer customer-managed log sinks.
[03:15] Rachel: somethings that trips us up is generation randomness; small model or decoding differences cause our downstream reranker to react. is there an option to pin model versions or fallback to a hosted variant?
[03:27] Alex: yes you can pin versions and setup fallbacks to compatible variants — e.g., if you pick a quantized variant for cost, you can fall back to a higher-precision one on mismatch. rollouts support canary and A/B as well.
[03:38] Tim: what about throughput numbers — any example numbers for, say, embeddings at scale? we do a nightly batch of 5M documents monthly inc ingestions so cost per embed matters.
[03:48] Jordan: we can share benchmark sheets but ballpark: Dedicated pools with mixed-precision quant can reduce embedding cost per unit significantly vs hosted; batching yields huge wins for embeddings — we usually see 3-5x throughput improvements when batch sizes are tuned. exact numbers depend on model and token length.
[04:06] Rachel: vendor lock-in concerns — we use some OpenAI-specific APIs, e.g., function-call-like patterns for structured output. can Redwood host managed function-calling or do we need to change prompts?
[04:17] Jordan: Redwood supports structured output and function-call patterns at the API layer; if you do custom wrappers we can map that behavior. there may be small interface differences but we often provide shim examples in SDKs.
[04:29] Laura: on compliance, if we went dedicated in cloud, do we get the same SOC2 coverage as Redwood hosted? any differences in attestations?
[04:38] Alex: the SOC2/ISO artifacts are the same for the control plane; for Private/on-prem deployments there are additional responsibilities on the customer side — we'll point out which controls are customer-managed. we'll include that matrix in the security pack.
[04:51] Tim: costs — can you give example pricing models for Dedicated? like committed monthly, vCPU/gpu pools, etc.
[04:59] Alex: committed capacity with monthly or annual commits. pricing typically is a mix of reserved GPU pool cost + per-request metering for ancillary services. we'll send a T-shirt estimate and a couple sample configs (small/medium/large pools) after this call.
[05:12] Rachel: great. another technical: do you support fine-tuning or adapters? we do few-shot + lightweight tuning in-house.
[05:19] Jordan: we support adapter-style personalization and fine-tune workflows in Dedicated; some customers prefer continuous-learning setups and we recommend a staging pipeline. we'll share docs.
[05:27] Rachel: ok last big Q — timeline and success criteria. we want a pilot in 6-8 weeks, with clear parity on quality and under 20% lower cost than OpenAI baseline for embeddings and 30% for generation at scale.
[05:39] Alex: reasonable. typical pilot: 4-6 weeks for initial eval parity + infra benchmark, then 6-12 weeks to production depending on integration complexity.
[05:47] Tim: what instrumentation will you provide for our engineers to compare outputs?
[05:52] Jordan: we'll provide token-level logs, per-request latency and cost breakdown, and a sample eval report. we can also run side-by-side evals in our benchmark harness.
[06:03] Laura: for KMS — do you allow bring-your-own KMS with cloud provider (AWS KMS) or do you force Redwood-managed keys?
[06:12] Alex: you can bring your own KMS (AWS/GCP/Azure) for Dedicated and Private, and we support HSM integrations for on-prem. we'll include integration notes.
[06:22] Rachel: sounds good. any major blockers we should know about?
[06:26] Jordan: usually the two sticking points are: 1) exact parity for very tuned OpenAI models — sometimes outputs differ and require prompt tweaks; 2) network/VPC setup if you pick Private, infra coordination is needed. both are manageable but we surface them early.
[06:41] Tim: ok that's fair. can you also include guidance on best quantization settings for balancing cost and hallucination risk?
[06:49] Jordan: yep, we'll provide recommendations per-model and per-workload. often 4-bit quant works well for embeddings and some generation, but for high-stakes outputs we suggest higher precision.
[06:59] Alex: recap and next steps: we'll send pricing + capacity options, security pack (SOC2/ISO/KMS matrix), Jordan will draft the benchmarking plan and we can schedule the deep-dive with your infra team next week (proposed 2026-05-27). Summit to share sample prompts, traffic profile and SLOs.
[07:18] Rachel: thanks, sounds actionable. one note — our legal/ procurement will need standard data processing addendum and terms; we'll loop them in soon.
[07:26] Alex: noted, we'll include DPAs and procurement points.
[07:29] Laura: thanks everyone.
[07:31] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up via email with docs and calendar invites.
